hook: Three households share a dark street. A streetlight would cost \$70 a year, and together they would gladly pay more than that for it. Yet weeks go by and nobody pays, because whoever pays lights the street for the neighbors too. Each one waits for someone else.

options: an outcome that is not socially efficient
a firm that earns a loss

figure.caption: Two questions sort every good: is it rival (does my use leave less for you)? Is it excludable (can nonpayers be kept out)?

chain.effect: people can enjoy it without paying

chain.effect: each waits for others to pay: free riding
a private seller cannot cover its cost, so the market provides too little or none

chain.cause: The total benefit still exceeds the cost
chain.effect: the outcome is inefficient, and government often provides the good, paid for with taxes

ideas: Rival: one person's use leaves less for others. Excludable: nonpayers can be kept out.
Private goods are rival and excludable; public goods nonrival and nonexcludable; common resources rival and nonexcludable; club goods nonrival and excludable.
Public goods suffer from the free-rider problem: markets underprovide them. A public good is worth providing when the sum of everyone's benefit is at least its cost.
Common resources are overused (the tragedy of the commons), because each user ignores the cost to others. Limits, permits or fees per unit reduce overuse.

misconception.wrong: A public good is any good the government provides.
misconception.right: A public good is defined by two features, nonrival and nonexcludable, not by who provides it. Governments provide many private goods (a public school lunch is rival), and some public goods are funded privately.

summary: Goods differ in rivalry (does one person's use leave less for others?) and excludability (can nonpayers be kept out?). Private goods are rival and excludable and markets handle them well. Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable: people can free ride, so markets provide too little, even when the sum of everyone's benefit exceeds the cost, and governments often provide them with taxes. Common resources are rival but nonexcludable, so they are overused. Club goods are excludable but nonrival.
